subject: ENG
label: Grade 04
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 04 English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 8 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Prose reading and main ideas
modules.outcome: summarise a passage and find evidence for an answer
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Prose reading and main ideas', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: summarise a passage and find evidence for an answer. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prose reading and main ideas' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: summarise a passage and find evidence for an answer, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Main idea in one sentence. Character: what they say and do shows what they are like (she gave away her lunch: generous). Drama: names on the left, stage directions in brackets. Method: Model run for 'Prose reading and main ideas'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.

modules.title: Prefixes and suffixes
modules.outcome: build and spell new words and say what they mean
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Prefixes and suffixes', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: build and spell new words and say what they mean. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prefixes and suffixes' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.

Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Prefix: dis + appear = disappear. Origins: telephone = Greek tele (far) + phone (sound); biology = bios (life) + logos (study). Method: Model run for 'Prefixes and suffixes'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Build and spell new words and say what they mean: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Start with a base word and a prefix. un- means not: happy becomes unhappy. re- means again: write becomes rewrite. dis- means not or opposite: agree becomes disagree. Reason: a prefix goes at the front and changes the meaning.

Step 2, Build with suffixes. -ful means full of: care becomes careful. -less means without: care becomes careless. -ly turns an adjective into an adverb: slow becomes slowly. Reason: a suffix goes at the end.
Step 3, Work out meanings by parts. "Unforgettable" = un- (not) + forget + -able (can be). Meaning: not able to be forgotten. Reason: splitting a word into parts reveals its meaning.

Step 4, Apply spelling rules. Drop silent e before -ing and -able: "hope" becomes "hoping". Change y to i before a suffix: "happy" becomes "happiness". Double the consonant in "run" before -ing: "running".
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "unhapyness". Right: "unhappiness" (un + happy, y to i, + ness). Another error: "carefull". Right: "careful" (the suffix is -ful with one l).

Step 6, Use new words in context. "The boy was careless and left his bag. His teacher was disappointed. He promised to recheck his work." Underline the prefix or suffix in each: careless, disappointed, recheck.

Step 7, Your turn. Build and define three words using un-, re- and -ful. Model answer: "unlock" (undo a lock); "retell" (tell again); "helpful" (full of help). Use one in a sentence: "She was helpful."

modules.outcome: use adverbs and prepositions to add detail
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Adverbs and prepositions', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: use adverbs and prepositions to add detail. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.

modules.example: Solved: 'The girl runs.' Add describing words: 'The tall girl runs fast.' Tense: walk, walked, will walk. Method: Model run for 'Adverbs and prepositions'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Use adverbs and prepositions to add detail: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Use adverbs to say how, when or where. "She spoke quietly." (how) "We left yesterday." (when) "He looked everywhere." (where) Reason: adverbs describe verbs.

Step 2, Change an adjective into an adverb with -ly. quick becomes quickly; careful becomes carefully; happy becomes happily. Irregular: good becomes well; fast stays fast. Model: "She runs fast and writes well."

Step 3, Use prepositions for position. "The cat is on the table." "The book is under the chair." "We walked across the bridge." Common ones: in, on, under, behind, between, through, across. Reason: they link a noun to the rest of the sentence.
Step 4, Add detail to a plain sentence. Plain: "The dog ran." Better: "The dog ran quickly across the yard and under the fence." Added adverb: quickly. Added prepositions: across, under.
Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "He plays good." Right: "He plays well." Another error: "She sat in front the door." Right: "She sat in front of the door." Remember: of follows "in front".

Step 6, Check position of adverbs. "Slowly, he opened the door." "He slowly opened the door." "He opened the door slowly." All work. Reason: adverbs of manner can move, but not between a verb and its object: not "He opened slowly the door".
Step 7, Your turn. Add one adverb and two prepositions: "The boy walked." Model answer: "The boy walked slowly along the path and through the gate."

modules.standard: Present, listen and respond with a reason: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Prepare a short presentation with an opening, two reasons and a close. Topic: "We should plant more trees." Opening: "Today I will explain why our school needs more trees."

Step 2, Give a reason with evidence. "First, trees give shade. On hot days, students can play outside because the playground is cooler." Reason: a reason plus an example is stronger than a claim alone.
Step 3, Add a second reason. "Second, trees clean the air, so everyone breathes easier." Link ideas with first, second and finally. Reason: signpost words help the audience follow.

Step 4, Listen and respond with a reason. Classmate: "Trees drop leaves and make a mess." You: "I understand your point, but we can collect leaves for compost, so the mess becomes useful." Reason: respond to the point, then add your reason.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak response: "No, you are wrong." Better: "I see it differently because shade protects students from the sun." Another error: reading the text word by word. Right: use key words and look at the audience.
Step 6, Close and invite questions. "To sum up, trees give shade and clean air, so we should plant more. Thank you. Are there any questions?" Reason: the summary repeats the main message.

Step 7, Your turn. Write one reason with because and one respectful response to a different view about the school library. Model answer: "We need a bigger library because many students share a few books." Response: "I see your point about cost, but books last for years."

ladder: L1: say and read familiar words and short sentences.
L2: read short texts and write connected sentences.
L3: write paragraphs and speak on a topic with notes.
L4: write for different purposes and analyse how texts persuade.
L5: write and argue at length; handle unseen texts.
L6 (degree): academic reading, writing and citation.
L7 (postgraduate): publish, teach or translate with expert accuracy.
